title: FinTech, Lesson 1: Take rate - where this product actually makes its money
subtitle: The four revenue sources of a digital financial product, and why a tiny percentage decides the whole model
whyItMatters: The first question in any product meeting at a fintech company is how much we keep on each transaction. Get that wrong and every forecast behind it is wrong too, because take rate multiplied by volume is the entire revenue line.
openingQuestion: An e-wallet processes 10,000bn of transactions a year at a take rate of 0.4%. What is the revenue?
openingOptions: 10,000bn, since all the volume flowing through the wallet is the wallet's revenue
explanation: Take rate is the share the company keeps of each unit flowing through the platform, not the whole amount that flows through. 10,000bn × 0.4% = 40bn. This is the most common error when reading a fintech company's accounts: transaction volume (GMV, TPV) is the number that makes the headline because it is large, but real revenue is only a very thin slice of it. A platform announcing TPV of 100,000bn at a take rate of 0.2% has revenue of 200bn - smaller than a mid-sized coffee chain. Conversely, a lending product with an effective take rate of 8-15% on balances only needs one percent of that volume to produce the same revenue.

diagram.label: Net revenue - the figure that is actually comparable

realWorldExample.description: Vietnam's three largest wallets all publish transaction volume and rarely publish a take rate. On bill payment and top-ups, the share kept is usually below 0.5% and a meaningful part of that still goes to the bank; which is why all three have pushed hard into lending, insurance and investment, where the retained margin is dozens of times higher.

quiz.question: What does take rate measure?
options: Total transaction value flowing through the platform
The share the platform keeps of each unit transacted
The share of users who return to the product in the following month
The share of transactions that fail and have to be refunded to customers
quiz.explanation: Take rate is revenue divided by transaction volume. Total transaction value is TPV or GMV, a completely different number and many times larger, and confusing the two is what produces revenue estimates that are off by two orders of magnitude. Return rate and failure rate are both real metrics, but neither has volume in the denominator in the way take rate does.

quiz.question: Platform A: TPV 50,000bn, take rate 0.3%. Platform B: TPV 3,000bn, take rate 9%. Which has higher revenue?
options: Equal, since the higher take rate offsets the lower volume
A, because its volume is 16 times larger than B's
B, with revenue of 270bn against A's 150bn
Cannot be determined without knowing the number of users
quiz.explanation: A: 50,000 × 0.3% = 150bn. B: 3,000 × 9% = 270bn. Large volume does not mean large revenue - which is exactly why payment wallets look for a route into credit products.

quiz.question: Why is net revenue the figure to use when comparing two fintech companies?
options: Because gross revenue only counts the transactions that succeeded
Because net revenue is always the larger figure and looks better in a report sent to investors
Because Vietnamese accounting standards prohibit publishing gross revenue
Because gross revenue still contains the amounts owed back to banks and card networks
quiz.explanation: With card payments, most of the fee collected from the customer flows straight to the card issuer as interchange. Two companies with the same gross revenue can be several times apart at the net level. Note that net revenue is by definition smaller than gross, not larger, and gross revenue is perfectly legal to publish - the problem is that it is not comparable across companies with different partner arrangements.

quiz.question: Which revenue source usually carries the highest effective take rate?
options: Consumer lending directly inside the wallet app
Phone top-ups and household utility bill payments
Transfers between users within the same wallet
QR code payments at small shops and food stalls
quiz.explanation: Interest and fees on loan balances typically leave a retained margin of 8-15%, while bill payment sits below 0.5% and internal transfers are close to zero. That is why almost every wallet ends up travelling the same road into credit. The payment lines all have the same problem: the fee is thin to begin with, and a large part of what is collected has to be shared with the bank.

quiz.question: A company announces 'GMV up 80%' while revenue is up only 12%. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The company is hiding revenue to reduce its tax liability for the period
Take rate is falling - the growth is coming from thin-margin products
GMV and revenue are unrelated, so the two cannot be compared at all
The figures must contain an error, since revenue has to grow in step with GMV
quiz.explanation: Revenue = GMV × take rate. GMV growing faster than revenue means the average take rate is thinning, usually because the growth is coming from a low-fee segment or because prices were cut to win share. The two are directly related by that identity, which is what makes the divergence informative rather than an error - and no tax strategy explains a published GMV figure.

practicePrompt.question: A platform has TPV of 40,000bn with a gross take rate of 1.2%, of which 0.85% has to be paid to banks and card networks. What is net revenue?
options: 620bn (= both take rates added)
practicePrompt.explanation: The net take rate is 1.2% − 0.85% = 0.35%, so net revenue is 140bn. The 480bn figure is real and is usually the one that reaches the press release, but nearly three quarters of it flows straight out to banks and card networks before the company keeps anything. Two fintech companies can only be compared at the net level, because the same business model can be reported gross or net depending on the standard applied - and the gap between the two presentations here is 3.4 times.

keyTakeaways: Revenue = transaction volume × take rate. Volume is the headline number; take rate is the one that decides the model.
Gross revenue less the amounts paid to banks and card networks gives net revenue - and only net figures are comparable.
Payments carry a thin take rate, credit is dozens of times fatter; almost every wallet takes that road.
GMV growing faster than revenue is the sign that take rate is being eroded.

summary.keyIdea: Revenue = transaction volume × take rate, and it is the second number that decides the model
summary.formula: Net revenue = GMV × take rate − costs paid to banks and card networks
summary.commonMistake: Comparing two companies on gross revenue, when the amounts they pay partners are wildly different.
summary.action: Take a listed fintech's accounts, divide revenue by GMV, and see whether that take rate is rising or falling across four quarters.

application.title: Compute the take rate of a product you use
application.message: Pick a wallet or a marketplace you use, find its published fee schedule, then estimate what percentage of each transaction it keeps after paying the bank.
application.secondary: If that number is below 0.5%, the model has to survive on enormous volume or on a different product entirely.

sections.text: Every fintech company likes to talk about transaction volume, because it is the largest number they have. But the volume flowing through the platform is not the platform's money - the share kept is.

Take rate is the ratio of revenue to transaction volume. A wallet processing 10,000bn at a take rate of 0.4% has revenue of 40bn. The 10,000bn figure is users' money moving from one account to another; the company only touches 0.4% of it.

sections.text: Four sources, four very different margins

sections.title: Where the revenue of a digital financial product comes from

concepts.def: Charged on each transfer, payment, top-up or withdrawal. Thin margin, usually below 1%, and much of it has to be shared with the bank.
Lending rate less cost of funds. The fattest margin, but it comes with credit risk - the high rate exists to cover what is never repaid.
Selling insurance, fund certificates or flight tickets through the app. No capital at risk, but entirely dependent on the user traffic already there.
A fixed monthly charge to businesses using the infrastructure. The steadiest and most forecastable, but slow to sell and needs a dedicated sales team.

sections.label: The usual confusion
sections.text: When reading a fintech company's accounts, always look for net revenue rather than stopping at gross. With card payments, most of the fee collected from the customer flows straight to the card issuer as interchange and never belongs to the company at all.

lines: Take rate multiplied by volume gives revenue - and of those two numbers, the small one is the one you control.
A platform wanting more revenue has only two roads: push volume up, or move users onto a product with a fatter margin. The next lesson is about the price of the first road.
